narrative.text: Introduces the WHO PrEP implementation tool, developed after WHO's 2015 recommendation to offer oral PrEP to people at substantial HIV risk. It stresses that individual risk varies, that people requesting PrEP should be prioritized, that barriers faced by key populations should be addressed and that the choice to use PrEP rests with the individual.
Explains that the PrEP tool is a set of modules for different stakeholders and that this STI integration module compiles existing WHO guidance without making new recommendations.
Sets out guiding principles for offering PrEP through a public health, human rights and people-centred approach and quotes WHO's definition of sexual health.

Introduces the module on integrating STI services with PrEP and lists in a box serious consequences of sexually transmitted infections such as congenital syphilis, HPV-related cancers, infertility and chronic hepatitis.

Gives global figures for curable STIs, estimating 374 million new cases in 2020, along with congenital syphilis, genital herpes and HPV-related cervical cancer, most occurring in low- and middle-income countries. It also explains that the module has two parts, for programme managers and for facility managers and health workers.

Reviews evidence that STI prevalence and incidence are high among people on PrEP, including men who have sex with men and young African women, compared with general population estimates. It discusses contributing factors such as sexual networks, condom use, stigma and background prevalence.

Explains the reasons for integrating STI services into PrEP, including reaching people with asymptomatic infections, efficiency gains, people-centred care and tackling antimicrobial resistance in gonorrhoea. It links integration to global targets for reducing STIs, congenital syphilis and cervical cancer deaths by 2030.
A section heading for Part 1 of the module, on integration of STI services for programme managers and other decision-makers.
Describes using the differentiated service delivery framework to plan which STI services to integrate with PrEP, and how, by whom and where they are offered.
Recommends a stepwise approach to integrating STI services with PrEP, adapted to local context and moving from symptom-based to cause-based management.
Explains that STI services should be added gradually and adapted to each PrEP delivery model, from digital to facility-based, with examples in an annex.
Notes that STI services chosen for integration must suit the PrEP delivery model and local resources, laws and regulations.

Discusses which health workers can deliver integrated PrEP and STI services, stressing task sharing with peers and lay providers, and shows a stepwise diagram from syndromic management to testing and vaccination. A case study describes integrated PrEP and STI services for key populations at a government health centre in Phnom Penh, Cambodia.

Describes the staffing and training needed to add STI services to PrEP delivery, such as training on diagnostic algorithms, case management and antimicrobial resistance. It also outlines the role of peers and community workers in linking clients to care and supporting adherence.

Argues that integrating PrEP and STI services can improve efficiency and draw HIV funding into the underfunded STI response, while noting extra costs for staff, training and supplies. It highlights the cost-effectiveness of dual HIV/syphilis tests and presents a Pan American Health Organization costing tool with an example comparing budget scenarios for 2021–2025.

Stresses documenting and monitoring STI services for PrEP users within existing reporting systems while protecting confidentiality, and points to suggested indicators. A case study from Namibia describes an online platform used to promote testing and manage HIV and STI services for key populations.

Explains the need to generate demand for STI services among PrEP users, since most STIs are asymptomatic, and to involve communities in designing messages. A case study describes a Brazilian project that used social media and a chatbot to reach adolescents from key populations.

Describes upcoming innovations that may ease integrated PrEP and STI services, including syphilis and dual HIV/syphilis self-tests, rapid tests for active syphilis and multiplex point-of-care platforms. It also mentions prevention innovations and vaccines and tests in development, noting WHO has not yet issued recommendations on them.

Opens Part 2 for facility managers and health workers, presenting an optimal package of STI services that can be integrated with PrEP and stressing that lack of STI services must never delay PrEP. It highlights the specific needs of adolescents and trans and gender diverse people and includes a schematic of STI case management.

Advises giving PrEP clients basic STI information, including self-assessment of symptoms, and reminding them that PrEP does not protect against other STIs. It notes that some symptoms have non-STI causes, such as candidiasis and bacterial vaginosis.

Defines counselling as a non-judgemental exchange that helps clients make informed decisions, noting that WHO does not recommend counselling aimed at changing behaviour. A box describes higher-risk practices such as chemsex and use of dating apps.

Stresses prompting clients to recognize STI signs and symptoms through self-assessment. A case study from South Africa describes adding symptom screening and a sub-study of laboratory STI testing to PrEP services for young people.

Summarizes WHO recommendations for STI prevention, mainly vaccines against hepatitis A, hepatitis B and HPV, and condoms with compatible lubricants. It notes the role of male circumcision and that post-exposure prophylaxis for bacterial STIs is recommended only after sexual assault.
Explains the options for STI testing, from laboratory and culture methods to rapid point-of-care and self-tests, and points to WHO laboratory guidance and prequalified diagnostics.

Discusses how often PrEP users should be tested for STIs, noting that self-testing and self-sampling can replace some visits and that evidence is insufficient for a general testing frequency. It suggests prioritizing regular testing for people at higher risk.

Explains the complexity of diagnosing syphilis and the differences between treponemal and non-treponemal serological tests and their limitations. It mentions dual rapid tests that may help identify active infection.

Discusses barriers to diagnosing gonorrhoea and chlamydia, such as the cost of molecular tests, and options like shared TB testing platforms and self-collected samples. It stresses sampling from the throat, rectum and genitals, citing studies showing many infections are missed otherwise, and includes a country example of pooled testing for key populations.

Recommends offering partner services to people who test positive for HIV or STIs and describes strategies such as user referral, provider referral and contract referral, noting their effectiveness when combined with dual HIV/syphilis testing.

Stresses the need for a private, supportive setting where clients can talk openly about their sexual history, which helps judge STI risk in PrEP services, while noting that history-taking should not be a condition for getting PrEP or STI care.

Sets out how to prepare for and conduct a respectful physical examination for STIs, with consent, privacy, a chaperone and the option of self-collected samples, and lists what to look for in the mouth, skin, genitals and anal area. A case study from Nigeria describes donor-supported cryotherapy for anogenital warts in one-stop clinics for key populations and the cost and liquid nitrogen problems that threaten its sustainability.

Explains the syndromic approach to STIs, which treats groups of symptoms for their most likely causes but can lead to both over- and undertreatment. It notes WHO's 2021 guideline recommends treatment based on molecular tests where possible and syndromic management where testing is limited, with flow charts for five syndromes.

Calls for correct STI treatment ideally on the first visit, rapid treatment of partners and counselling on medicines and adherence, using standard protocols to limit antimicrobial resistance. It points to WHO treatment guidelines for chlamydia, herpes, gonorrhoea, syphilis, syphilis in pregnancy and HPV-related cervical lesions.

Explains that clinical follow-up is mainly for people whose symptoms persist after treatment and lists reasons for treatment failure, such as poor adherence, reinfection, antimicrobial resistance and other untreated infections. Footnotes note that WHO is revising gonorrhoea treatment because of growing resistance.

Discusses referral of people with STIs to other levels of care and the risk of losing them to follow-up, which makes same-day treatment especially valuable. It lists strategies to support linkage, such as non-judgemental and flexible services, self-collection, free care, peer support, digital tools and clear national policies. A case study from South Africa describes client preferences, showing most favour self-led STI services but some prefer provider-led care, so services should offer choice.

Describes rising outbreaks of syphilis, gonorrhoea including extensively drug-resistant strains, lymphogranuloma venereum, HIV and other sexually transmissible infections such as Shigella, E. coli, hepatitis A, B and C and monkeypox, reported mainly among men who have sex with men in high-income countries. A box sets out how monkeypox spreads, its symptoms and differential diagnosis, contact tracing and vaccination of contacts soon after exposure. It ends by warning against stigmatizing affected groups and noting that PrEP services can help detect and report surges in infections.

The reference list for the module on integrating STI services into PrEP, citing mainly WHO guidelines on PrEP, HIV, STIs, hepatitis and key populations, along with research on STI epidemiology, service preferences and monkeypox vaccination.

Lists the WHO guidelines and guidance this STI integration module aligns with, grouped by key populations, STIs, cervical cancer, viral hepatitis and strategic information, with their full references. These include guidelines on symptomatic STI management, self-collection of samples, syphilis in pregnancy, treatment of specific STIs, cervical pre-cancer screening and hepatitis B and C testing and care.

Presents a table showing which STI services, such as counselling, partner services, rapid tests, self-sampling, molecular testing, vaccination, treatment and referral, could be offered through different PrEP delivery models, from virtual platforms and home delivery to pharmacies, mobile units and facilities with or without laboratories. Notes explain the abbreviations and that implementation depends on local context and national rules.

Sets out core STI indicators for PrEP and HIV services, giving short names, definitions, numerators and denominators for testing coverage, test positivity and treatment coverage for syphilis, gonorrhoea and other infections. It also includes an indicator on STI incidence among people using PrEP measured per person-years and cites WHO strategic information guidelines. Each indicator is designed to be tracked over a reporting period.

Tabulates the main pathogens relevant to people using PrEP, such as chlamydia, herpes, genital mycoplasmas, hepatitis A, B and C, HPV, lymphogranuloma venereum, gonorrhoea, syphilis and trichomonas, showing whether each is curable and how it is transmitted. Footnotes clarify points such as suppressive therapy for herpes and hepatitis B.

Summarises WHO-recommended diagnostic tests and first-line treatments for selected sexually transmissible pathogens, including chlamydia, herpes, Mycoplasma genitalium, hepatitis B and C, gonorrhoea and syphilis. It gives drug regimens and notes such as pooling samples from three sites, preferring doxycycline for anorectal chlamydia and avoiding it in pregnancy. The table's WHO guideline references and contact details for WHO's global HIV, hepatitis and STI programmes close the document.

The cover, copyright page and table of contents of Module 13 of the WHO implementation tool for HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), on integrating STI services, listing sections for programme managers and health workers and annexes on pathogens and testing guidance.
